Point Convergence of Nesterov’s Accelerated Gradient Method: An AI-Assisted Proof

Uijeong Jang ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles.
e-mail: <uijeongjang@math.ucla.edu> and <eryu@math.ucla.edu>    Ernest K. Ryu11footnotemark: 1
Abstract

The Nesterov accelerated gradient method, introduced in 1983, has been a cornerstone of optimization theory and practice. Yet the question of its point convergence had remained open. In this work, we resolve this longstanding open problem in the affirmative. The discovery of the proof was heavily assisted by ChatGPT, a proprietary large language model, and we describe the process through which its assistance was elicited.

1 Introduction

Consider the optimization problem

minimizex∈ℝnf⁡(x),\begin{array}[]{ll}\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}{\mbox{minimize}}&f(x),\end{array}

where f:ℝn→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is LL-smooth and convex. The plain gradient descent method, whose origin dates back to Cauchy [7], is

xk+1=xk−1L∇f(xk)x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f(x_{k})

for k=0,1,…k=0,1,\dots with x0∈ℝnx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Gradient descent is known to converge in the sense of xk→x∞∈arg​min⁡fx_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty}\in\argmin f and f⁡(xk)−inff≤𝒪⁡(1/k)f(x_{k})-\inf f\leq\mathcal{O}(1/k) [3]. However, the 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}(1/k) rate is famously suboptimal and can be accelerated. Nesterov’s 1983 seminal paper [9] presented the Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG) method

xk+1\displaystyle x_{k+1} =yk−1L∇f(yk),\displaystyle=y_{k}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_{k}),
yk+1\displaystyle y_{k+1} =xk+1+tk−1tk+1​(xk+1−xk)\displaystyle=x_{k+1}+\frac{t_{k}-1}{t_{k+1}}(x_{k+1}-x_{k})

for k=0,1,…k=0,1,\dots with x0=y0∈ℝnx_{0}=y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, t0=1t_{0}=1, and tk+12−tk+1≤tk2t_{k+1}^{2}-t_{k+1}\leq t_{k}^{2}. NAG is known to converge in the sense of f⁡(xk)−inff≤𝒪⁡(1/k2)f(x_{k})-\inf f\leq\mathcal{O}(1/k^{2}), an accelerated rate, when tk+1=(1+1+4​tk2)/2t_{k+1}=(1+\sqrt{1+4t_{k}^{2}})/2 or tk=(k+2)/2t_{k}=(k+2)/2 for k=0,1,…k=0,1,\dots. However, whether NAG exhibits point convergence xk→x∞∈arg​min⁡fx_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty}\in\argmin f has remained an open problem.

In this work, we resolve this longstanding open problem in the affirmative by showing point convergence for NAG in the sense of

xk→x∞,yk→x∞,x∞∈arg​min⁡f.x_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty},\qquad y_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty},\qquad x_{\infty}\in\argmin f.

The discovery of the proof was heavily assisted by ChatGPT, a proprietary large language model, and we describe the process through which its assistance was elicited.

This result, along with the use of AI in its discovery, was first announced by the authors on X.com, a social networking platform, where it received significant public attention. Given the level of interest, we are quickly releasing this archival record to formally document the proofs and facilitate their prompt dissemination. An updated version of this manuscript, offering a more detailed discussion of the historical context and relevant prior work, will be released in due course.

1.1 Notation

A function f:ℝn→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is convex if

f⁡(θ​x+(1−θ)​y)≤θ​f​(x)+(1−θ)​f​(y),∀x,y∈ℝn,θ∈[0,1].f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\leq\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y),\qquad\forall\,x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\,\theta\in[0,1].

If f:ℝn→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is differentiable and convex, then it satisfies the convexity inequality [11, Equation 2.1.2]

f⁡(y)≥f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩,∀x,y∈ℝn.f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle,\qquad\forall\,x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

For L>0L>0, we say f:ℝn→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is LL-smooth if ff is differentiable and

‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖≤L​‖x−y‖∀x,y∈ℝn.\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad\forall\,x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

If f:ℝn→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is LL-smooth and convex, then it satisfies the cocoercivity inequality [11, Theorem 2.1.5]

f⁡(y)≥f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩+12​L​‖∇f​(y)−∇f​(x)‖2,∀x,y∈ℝn.f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x)\|^{2},\qquad\forall\,x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Write arg​min⁡f\argmin f to denote the set of minimizers of ff and f⋆=infx∈ℝnff_{\star}=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}f to denote the minimum value.

1.2 Concurrent work

The results presented in this manuscript were first announced by the authors on X.com through a series of daily posts from October 21 to October 24, 2025. Specifically, the convergence of the continuous-time dynamics for the case r=3r=3 was announced on October 21, and the convergence of the discrete-time NAG method was announced on October 24.

On October 24, the authors of [6] contacted us, the authors of this work, with a manuscript also establishing point convergence of the discrete-time NAG. Their work builds upon the initial X.com post made on October 21 but was conducted independently of the October 24 post.

Beyond the analysis of NAG, the manuscript [6] contains additional results that do not overlap with the results of this work: their analysis extends to the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space setting, and they further argue that the FISTA method [4] also exhibits point convergence.

2 Point convergence in continuous time

Let f:ℝn→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a differentiable convex function with at least one minimizer. Consider the generalized Nesterov ODE

X¨​(t)+rt​X˙​(t)+∇f​(X⁡(t))=0,for ​t>0\ddot{X}(t)+\frac{r}{t}\dot{X}(t)+\nabla f\big(X(t)\big)=0,\qquad\text{for }t>0

with r>0r>0 and initial conditions X⁡(0)=X0X(0)=X_{0} and X˙​(0)=0\dot{X}(0)=0. The goal is to determine whether

X⁡(t)→X∞∈arg​min⁡fX(t)\rightarrow X_{\infty}\in\argmin f

holds, or whether there is an f:ℝn→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that {X⁡(t)}t≥0\{X(t)\}_{t\geq 0} diverges. We take for granted the existence of a global solution to the ODE.

Prior work [2] has shown convergence for the overdamped regime r>3r>3. In the following, we establish convergence for the critical damping regime r=3r=3, which is the main case of interest, provide a partial convergence result for r∈(1,3)r\in(1,3), and demonstrate divergence for r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1].

For z∈arg​min⁡fz\in\argmin f, consider the following energy function:

The energy function ℰz​(t)\mathcal{E}_{z}(t) converges to a finite limit and X⁡(t)X(t) is bounded for all tt.

∎

Theorem 2.

The solution X⁡(t)X(t) of the Nesterov ODE converges to a minimizer. That is,

X⁡(t)→X∞∈arg​min⁡f.X(t)\rightarrow X_{\infty}\in\argmin f.
Proof.

Since {X⁡(t)}t≥0⊂ℝn\{X(t)\}_{t\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is bounded, the dynamics have at least one cluster point. Since f⁡(X⁡(t))→f⋆f(X(t))\rightarrow f_{\star} and ff is continuous, all cluster points attain the function value f⋆f_{\star} and therefore are minimizers. If there is only one cluster point, X⁡(t)X(t) converges to a limit, and we are done.

Therefore, assume z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are cluster points of X⁡(t)X(t), so z1,z2∈arg​min⁡fz_{1},z_{2}\in\argmin f. We will now show z1=z2z_{1}=z_{2}. Let

hi​(t):=‖X⁡(t)−zi‖2​ for ​i=1,2,H⁡(t):=ℰz1​(t)−ℰz2​(t).h_{i}(t):=\|X(t)-z_{i}\|^{2}\textup{ for }i=1,2\,,\qquad H(t):=\mathcal{E}_{z_{1}}(t)-\mathcal{E}_{z_{2}}(t).

Expanding the square in ℰz\mathcal{E}_{z} gives

ℰz​(t)=t2​(f⁡(X)−f⋆)+12​t2​‖X˙‖2+2​hz​(t)+t​hz′​(t).\mathcal{E}_{z}(t)=t^{2}\big(f(X)-f_{\star}\big)+\tfrac{1}{2}t^{2}\|\dot{X}\|^{2}+2h_{z}(t)+t\,h_{z}^{\prime}(t).

t​(h1−h2)′+2​(h1−h2)=H⁡(t).t\,(h_{1}-h_{2})^{\prime}+2(h_{1}-h_{2})=H(t). (1)

Since both ℰz1​(t)\mathcal{E}_{z_{1}}(t) and ℰz2​(t)\mathcal{E}_{z_{2}}(t) converge to finite limits,

H⁡(t)→H⁡(∞)<∞.H(t)\to H(\infty)<\infty.

Multiply (1) by the integrating factor tt to obtain

dd​t​(t2​(h1​(t)−h2​(t)))=t​H​(t).\frac{d}{dt}(t^{2}(h_{1}(t)-h_{2}(t)))=t\,H(t).

Then

(t2​(h1​(t)−h2​(t)))−(t02​(h1​(t0)−h2​(t0)))=∫0ts​H​(s)​𝑑s,(t^{2}(h_{1}(t)-h_{2}(t)))-(t_{0}^{2}(h_{1}(t_{0})-h_{2}(t_{0})))=\int_{0}^{t}sH(s)ds,

which implies

h1​(t)−h2​(t)=t02t2​(h1​(t0)−h2​(t0))+1t2​∫0ts​H​(s)​𝑑s.h_{1}(t)-h_{2}(t)=\frac{t_{0}^{2}}{t^{2}}(h_{1}(t_{0})-h_{2}(t_{0}))+\frac{1}{t^{2}}\int_{0}^{t}sH(s)ds.

By taking t→∞t\to\infty, the first term on the right-hand side vanishes and the second terms converges to H⁡(∞)2\frac{H(\infty)}{2} by L’Hôpital’s rule. Thus, h1​(t)−h2​(t)h_{1}(t)-h_{2}(t) converges. Evaluating h1−h2h_{1}-h_{2} along two subsequences {tk}k≥0\{t_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} and {sk}k≥0\{s_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} such that X⁡(tk)→z1X(t_{k})\rightarrow z_{1} and X⁡(sk)→z2X(s_{k})\rightarrow z_{2} respectively, we get

limk→∞(h1​(tk)−h2​(tk))=‖z1−z1‖2−‖z1−z2‖2=−‖z1−z2‖2\lim_{k\to\infty}(h_{1}(t_{k})-h_{2}(t_{k}))=\|z_{1}-z_{1}\|^{2}-\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|^{2}=-\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|^{2}

and

limk→∞(h1​(sk)−h2​(sk))=‖z2−z1‖2−‖z2−z2‖2=‖z2−z1‖2\lim_{k\to\infty}(h_{1}(s_{k})-h_{2}(s_{k}))=\|z_{2}-z_{1}\|^{2}-\|z_{2}-z_{2}\|^{2}=\|z_{2}-z_{1}\|^{2}

The two values must coincide since h1−h2h_{1}-h_{2} has a limit, therefore z1=z2z_{1}=z_{2}. ∎

Theorem 4 (Uniqueness of the limit for r∈(1,3)r\in(1,3)).

2.3 Divergence for r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1]

In the following, we present a counterexample showing that point convergence does not hold in general for r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1].

Theorem 5.

Let f:ℝ→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be given by

f⁡(x)={12​(x−1)2x>10|x|≤112​(x+1)2x<−1.f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\tfrac{1}{2}(x-1)^{2}&x>1\\ 0&|x|\leq 1\\ \tfrac{1}{2}(x+1)^{2}&x<-1.\end{array}\right.

and consider

The equation is piecewise linear and can be written in three parts as follows: If x⁡(t)>1x(t)>1, let y⁡(t)=x⁡(t)−1y(t)=x(t)-1. Then

y¨+rt​y˙+y=0.\ddot{y}+\frac{r}{t}\dot{y}+y=0. (R)

If |x⁡(t)|≤1|x(t)|\leq 1, we have

If x⁡(t)<−1x(t)<-1, let z⁡(t)=x⁡(t)+1z(t)=x(t)+1. Then

We will show that the trajectory hits x=1x=1 and x=−1x=-1 infinitely many times, and hence cannot converge.

Consider equation (R) (the same argument applies to (L)). Let y(t)=t−r/2u(t)y(t)=t^{-r/2}u(t); a short calculation yields

u¨+(1+r⁡(2−r)4​t2)​u=0.\ddot{u}+\Bigl(1+\frac{r(2-r)}{4t^{2}}\Bigr)u=0. (⋆\star)

Because r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1], the coefficient in ( ⋆ ‣ 2.3) satisfies

1+r⁡(2−r)4​t2≥1for all ​t>0.1+\frac{r(2-r)}{4t^{2}}\geq 1\qquad\text{for all }t>0.

By the Sturm comparison theorem with w=sin⁡tw=\sin t satisfying w¨+w=0\ddot{w}+w=0, every nontrivial solution uu of ( ⋆ ‣ 2.3) (and hence every nontrivial yy of (R)) has a zero in every interval of length at most π\pi.

In particular, starting outside with y⁡(t0)>0y(t_{0})>0 (or equivalently x⁡(t0)>1x(t_{0})>1), there exists a first time t1>0t_{1}>0 such that y⁡(t1)=0y(t_{1})=0; that is, x⁡(t1)=1x(t_{1})=1. Thus, x˙​(t1)≠0\dot{x}(t_{1})\neq 0 and the trajectory enters the region |x|<1|x|<1 with strictly negative velocity. In this section, we establish point convergence of the following discrete-time methods: Nesterov’s 1983 NAG method [9] and Kim and Fessler’s 2016 optimized gradient method [8].

3.1 Nesterov accelerated gradient

Consider the Nesterov accelerated gradient algorithm (NAG)

xk+1\displaystyle x_{k+1} =yk−1L∇f(yk),\displaystyle=y_{k}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_{k}),

The sequence {xk}k≥0\{x_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} produced by NAG is bounded.

Lemma 9 ([5, Lemma A.4]).

Let {hk}k≥0⊂ℝ\{h_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{R} and {φk}k≥0⊂ℝ\{\varphi_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{R} be sequences of real and positive numbers respectively, and such that ∑k=0∞1φk=∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\varphi_{k}}=\infty. Then if

Theorem 10.

The sequences {xk}k≥0\{x_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} and {yk}k≥0\{y_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} of NAG converge to the same minimizer. That is,

xk→x∞,yk→x∞,x∞∈arg​min⁡f.x_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty},\qquad y_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty},\qquad x_{\infty}\in\argmin f.

3.2 Optimized gradient method

Consider the optimized gradient method (OGM)

xk+1\displaystyle x_{k+1} =yk−1L∇f(yk),\displaystyle=y_{k}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_{k}),
yk+1\displaystyle y_{k+1} =xk+1+θk−1θk+1​(xk+1−xk)+θkθk+1​(xk+1−yk)\displaystyle=x_{k+1}+\frac{\theta_{k}-1}{\theta_{k+1}}(x_{k+1}-x_{k})+\frac{\theta_{k}}{\theta_{k+1}}(x_{k+1}-y_{k})

for k=0,1,…k=0,1,\dots with x0=y0∈ℝnx_{0}=y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and a nonnegative sequence {θk}k=0,1,…\{\theta_{k}\}_{k=0,1,\dots} satisfying θ0=1\theta_{0}=1 and θk+12−θk+1=θk2\theta_{k+1}^{2}-\theta_{k+1}=\theta_{k}^{2} for k=0,1,…k=0,1,\dots. For notational convenience, also define θ−1=0\theta_{-1}=0.

Lemma 11 ([8, Proposition 5]).

The following is equivalent to OGM in the sense that it produces the same sequences {xk}k≥0\{x_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} and {yk}k≥0\{y_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}:

zk+1\displaystyle z_{k+1} =zk−2​θkL∇f(yk)\displaystyle=z_{k}-\frac{2\theta_{k}}{L}\nabla f(y_{k})

for k=0,1,…k=0,1,\dots, where x0=y0=z0∈ℝnx_{0}=y_{0}=z_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Lemma 12 ([12, Theorem 1]).

For x⋆∈arg​min⁡fx_{\star}\in\argmin f, consider the following energy function for k≥0k\geq 0:

ℰk​(x⋆)=2​θk2​(f⁡(yk)−f⋆−12​L​‖∇f​(yk)‖2⏟≥0, by cocoercivity )+L2​‖zk+1−x⋆‖2\mathcal{E}_{k}(x_{\star})=2\theta_{k}^{2}\big(\underbrace{f(y_{k})-f_{\star}-\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla f(y_{k})\|^{2}}_{\geq 0,\textup{ by cocoercivity }}\big)+\frac{L}{2}\|z_{k+1}-x_{\star}\|^{2}

where y−1=y0y_{-1}=y_{0} and z−1=z0z_{-1}=z_{0}. Then ℰk+1​(x⋆)≤ℰk​(x⋆)\mathcal{E}_{k+1}(x_{\star})\leq\mathcal{E}_{k}(x_{\star}) for all k=−1,0,1,2,…k=-1,0,1,2,\dots, hence {ℰk​(x⋆)}k≥−1\{\mathcal{E}_{k}(x_{\star})\}_{k\geq-1} converges to a finite limit.

Lemma 13.

The sequences {xk}k≥0\{x_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} and {yk}k≥0\{y_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} produced by OGM are bounded.

Proof.

From the OGM updates, we have

xk+1=yk+zk+1−zk2​θk,yk+1=(1−1θk+1)​xk+1+1θk+1​zk+1.x_{k+1}=y_{k}+\frac{z_{k+1}-z_{k}}{2\theta_{k}},\qquad y_{k+1}=\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr)x_{k+1}+\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}z_{k+1}.

By Lemma 12, {zk}\{z_{k}\} is bounded, i.e., supk‖zk‖≤M\sup_{k}\|z_{k}\|\leq M. Then,

‖xk+1‖\displaystyle\|x_{k+1}\| ≤‖yk‖+‖zk+1‖+‖zk‖2​θk≤‖yk‖+Mθk,\displaystyle\leq\|y_{k}\|+\frac{\|z_{k+1}\|+\|z_{k}\|}{2\theta_{k}}\leq\|y_{k}\|+\frac{M}{\theta_{k}}, (4)
‖yk+1‖\displaystyle\|y_{k+1}\| ≤(1−1θk+1)​‖xk+1‖+Mθk+1.\displaystyle\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr)\|x_{k+1}\|+\frac{M}{\theta_{k+1}}. (5)

‖yk+1‖≤(1−1θk+1)​‖yk‖+M⁡(1θk+1+1θk​(1−1θk+1)).\|y_{k+1}\|\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr)\|y_{k}\|+M\Bigl(\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}+\frac{1}{\theta_{k}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr)\Bigr).

Since θk+1≤θk+1\theta_{k+1}\leq\theta_{k}+1,

1θk+1+1θk​(1−1θk+1)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}+\frac{1}{\theta_{k}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr) =1θk+1+1θk−1θk​θk+1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}+\frac{1}{\theta_{k}}-\frac{1}{\theta_{k}\theta_{k+1}}
=1θk+1+θk+1−1θk​θk+1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}+\frac{\theta_{k+1}-1}{\theta_{k}\theta_{k+1}}
≤1θk+1+θkθk​θk+1\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}+\frac{\theta_{k}}{\theta_{k}\theta_{k+1}}

‖yk+1‖≤(1−1θk+1)​‖yk‖+2​Mθk+1.\|y_{k+1}\|\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr)\|y_{k}\|+\frac{2M}{\theta_{k+1}}. (6)

‖yk+1‖≤(1−1θk+1)​B+2​Mθk+1≤(1−1θk+1)​B+Bθk+1=B,\|y_{k+1}\|\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr)B+\frac{2M}{\theta_{k+1}}\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{k+1}}\Bigr)B+\frac{B}{\theta_{k+1}}=B,

since 2​M≤B2M\leq B. Thus, by induction, {yk}k≥0\{y_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} is bounded. Finally, by (4),

Theorem 14.

The sequences {xk}k≥0\{x_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} and {yk}k≥0\{y_{k}\}_{k\geq 0} of OGM converge to the same minimizer. That is,

xk→x∞,yk→x∞,x∞∈arg​min⁡f.x_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty},\qquad y_{k}\rightarrow x_{\infty},\qquad x_{\infty}\in\argmin f.
Proof.

Since {xk}k≥0⊂ℝn\{x_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is bounded, the dynamics have at least one cluster point. Also,

2​θk−12​(f⁡(xk)−f⋆)\displaystyle 2\theta_{k-1}^{2}\bigl(f(x_{k})-f_{\star}\bigr) ≤ 2​θk−12​(f⁡(yk−1)−f⋆−12​L​‖∇f​(yk−1)‖2)\displaystyle\;\leq\;2\theta_{k-1}^{2}\!\left(f(y_{k-1})-f_{\star}-\frac{1}{2L}\,\|\nabla f(y_{k-1})\|^{2}\right)
≤ℰk−1​(x⋆)≤ℰ−1​(x⋆)=L2​‖z0−x⋆‖2.\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{E}_{k-1}(x_{\star})\;\leq\;\mathcal{E}_{-1}(x_{\star})\;=\;\frac{L}{2}\,\|z_{0}-x_{\star}\|^{2}.

Together with θk→∞\theta_{k}\to\infty implies f⁡(xk)→f⋆f(x_{k})\to f_{\star}. Hence, all cluster points attain the function value f⋆f_{\star} and therefore are minimizers. As in the NAG case, let x⋆,x~⋆∈arg⁡min⁡fx_{\star},\tilde{x}_{\star}\in\arg\min f be two cluster points of {xk}k≥0\{x_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}. Let

hkx:=‖xk−x⋆‖2−‖xk−x~⋆‖2,hky:=‖yk−x⋆‖2−‖yk−x~⋆‖2,h_{k}^{x}:=\|x_{k}-x_{\star}\|^{2}-\|x_{k}-\tilde{x}_{\star}\|^{2},\qquad h_{k}^{y}:=\|y_{k}-x_{\star}\|^{2}-\|y_{k}-\tilde{x}_{\star}\|^{2},

and

Hk:=ℰk​(x⋆)−ℰk​(x~⋆).H_{k}:=\mathcal{E}_{k}(x_{\star})-\mathcal{E}_{k}(\tilde{x}_{\star}).

From the definition of ℰk​(x⋆)\mathcal{E}_{k}(x_{\star}), the only dependence on x⋆x_{\star} is through ‖zk−x‖2\|z_{k}-x\|^{2}, so for any x⋆,x~⋆∈arg⁡min⁡fx_{\star},\tilde{x}_{\star}\in\arg\min f we have

2L​Hk+1=−2​⟨zk+1,x⋆−x~⋆⟩+‖x⋆‖2−‖x~⋆‖2.\frac{2}{L}H_{k+1}=-2\langle z_{k+1},\,x_{\star}-\tilde{x}_{\star}\rangle+\|x_{\star}\|^{2}-\|\tilde{x}_{\star}\|^{2}.

θk+1​yk+1−(θk+1−1)​xk+1=zk+1,\theta_{k+1}y_{k+1}-(\theta_{k+1}-1)x_{k+1}=z_{k+1},

and the relations

−2​⟨xk+1,x⋆−x~⋆⟩=hk+1x−‖x⋆‖2+‖x~⋆‖2,−2​⟨yk+1,x⋆−x~⋆⟩=hk+1y−‖x⋆‖2+‖x~⋆‖2,-2\langle x_{k+1},\,x_{\star}-\tilde{x}_{\star}\rangle=h_{k+1}^{x}-\|x_{\star}\|^{2}+\|\tilde{x}_{\star}\|^{2},\qquad-2\langle y_{k+1},\,x_{\star}-\tilde{x}_{\star}\rangle=h_{k+1}^{y}-\|x_{\star}\|^{2}+\|\tilde{x}_{\star}\|^{2},

θk+1​hk+1x−(θk+1−1)​hk+1y=2L​Hk+1.\theta_{k+1}h_{k+1}^{x}-(\theta_{k+1}-1)h_{k+1}^{y}=\frac{2}{L}H_{k+1}. (7)

hk+1y=hkx+1L​θk​(Hk+1−Hk).h_{k+1}^{y}=h_{k}^{x}+\frac{1}{L\theta_{k}}(H_{k+1}-H_{k}). (8)

4 Eliciting AI-assistance

The discovery of the proofs presented in this work was heavily assisted by ChatGPT, a proprietary large language model. We believe that the mathematical results presented in this work hold value independent of the method of their discovery. At the same time, we believe our discovery serves as a case study demonstrating how AI can be leveraged to accelerate the discovery of new mathematics. For this reason, we briefly describe the process through which ChatGPT’s assistance was elicited.

The process began by prompting ChatGPT to solve the continuous-time problem. The model did not produce the correct answer in a single attempt; rather, the process was highly interactive. ChatGPT generated numerous arguments, approximately 80% of which were incorrect, but several ideas felt novel and worth further exploring. Whenever a new idea emerged, whether correct or only partially so, we distilled the key insight and prompted ChatGPT to develop it further.

The authors’ contribution was to filter out incorrect arguments, consolidate a consistent set of valid facts, identify promising lines of reasoning, and determine when a particular approach had been fully explored. ChatGPT’s contribution was to generate candidate arguments, substantially accelerate the exploration of potential avenues, particularly by quickly ruling out unproductive directions, and ultimately produce the final proof argument.

Once the proof for the continuous-time setting with r=3r=3 was discovered, the extensions to r∈(1,3)r\in(1,3) and the translation to the discrete-time Nesterov accelerated gradient method were relatively straightforward. The prompting technique was to provide the proof for the continuous-time case in LaTeX code, presenting the desired extension as a theorem statement, and instructing ChatGPT to produce a proof of the new theorem using ideas from the supplied proof.

For the case r∈(1,3)r\in(1,3) in continuous-time, however, we were not able to establish boundedness in full generality. We prompted ChatGPT to prove the boundedness of {X⁡(t)}t≥t0\{X(t)\}_{t\geq t_{0}}, suggesting several potentially promising approaches, but the model was unable to produce a valid proof. We then carefully re-examined the problem ourselves to ensure that no simple argument had been overlooked. After a reasonable amount of effort, we concurred with ChatGPT that the technique used for establishing boundedness for the case r=3r=3 does not immediately extend to the case r<3r<3. We therefore leave this issue as an open problem.
